sections.heading: 4.1 Learning Process
sections.text: Table 2 illustrates the learning trajectory using Llama3.2 as a representative example. Other models exhibit similar trends. Starting from an empty rule library, we collect failure traces from a zero-shot agent and generate candidate rules, yielding 72 rules on ToolHop and 151 on BFCL 9 9 9 See Appendix for sample rules . This initial rule set improves accuracy on both test-rand and test-unseen splits. Applying MDL-guided consolidation further reduces the rule count (by 7% on ToolHop and 20% on BFCL) while improving performance on test-rand and yielding smaller but consistent gains on test-unseen. Overall, the process produces a compact, interpretable rule library that improves both in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization.

sections.heading: 4.2 Case Study
sections.text: Table 6 shows a representative failure where the agent directly queries a complex familial relationship, leading to a tool error. RimRule identifies the root cause as improper decomposition and induces a rule that enforces stepwise resolution of intermediate entities. The resulting rule is abstract and reusable, and its symbolic form enables reliable retrieval for similar queries. This example illustrates how failure traces are converted into compact rules that correct systematic reasoning errors beyond the original instance. Table 6: Case study illustrating failure-driven rule induction and symbolic representation. Query How many letters (excluding the first and last) are there in the first name of Viacheslav I of Kiev’s maternal grandfather? Failure The agent directly queries Viacheslav I of Kiev’s maternal grandfather . The tool returns an error: “no data found” . Proposed Rule If the user query involves identifying a specific familial relationship (e.g., maternal grandfather), then decompose the task by first resolving intermediate relationships (e.g., mother, father) sequentially. Symbolic Form if domain=FAMILIAL_RELATIONSHIP or tool_category=GENEALOGY_QUERY , then action=[DECOMPOSE_QUERY, RESOLVE_INTERMEDIATE_ENTITY, SEQUENCE_SUBTASKS] strength=MANDATORY

sections.heading: 4.3 Re-usability Across LLMs
sections.text: Humans can share heuristics because they are interpretable across contexts. By encoding adaptation as symbolic, human-readable rules, our method enables knowledge to be reused across LLMs without retraining. We learn two rule libraries from failure traces produced by Llama3.2 and GPT-4o , and apply them to models of varying size and reasoning strength, evaluating performance on the test-rand split. Table 3 shows consistent gains in both directions: strong-to-weak transfer improves smaller models, while weak-to-strong transfer benefits strong reasoning models such as O1 and Llama4 . These results suggest that symbolic rules capture transferable failure patterns not resolved by scale alone. Table 7: Test-rand accuracy (\pm standard deviation, in %) comparing retrieval strategies. sections.heading: 4.4 Performance on Small Dataset
sections.text: We evaluate RimRule in a low-resource setting on the multi_turn_base split of BFCL using only 90 training samples. Despite limited supervision, the method learns just four rules (Appendix A.2 ) yet achieves substantial gains: accuracy improves from 55.2\% to 62.1\% on test-rand and from 46.0\% to 60.0\% on test-unseen. These results highlight the sample efficiency and practical applicability of rule-based adaptation.

sections.heading: 4.5 Outperforming Prompting-based Methods
sections.text: We compare RimRule against prompting-based adaptation methods, including zero-shot prompting ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , few-shot in-context learning ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , and prompt optimization with SEE ( Cui et al., 2025 ) . As shown in Table 4 , RimRule consistently outperforms all prompting baselines on both ToolHop and BFCL, across test-rand and test-unseen splits, demonstrating stronger generalization than fixed-prompt approaches.

sections.heading: 4.6 Complementing Finetuned Models
sections.text: As shown in Table 5 , adding RimRule to finetuned models yields consistent gains, especially on the test-unseen split, indicating that symbolic rules correct residual systematic errors left by supervised training. We observe similar improvements when applying RimRule to models with native function-calling capabilities (Table 5 ), showing that rule-based adaptation operates along an orthogonal axis of generalization. sections.text: Impact of retrieval method. Table 7 shows that symbolic retrieval consistently outperforms retrieval based on raw natural-language similarity on both datasets. Impact of consolidation method. As shown in Table 8 , MDL-guided consolidation significantly outperforms prompt-based rule merging. Together, these results indicate that both symbolic retrieval and MDL-based consolidation are essential to our approach.

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Rule Learning with LLMs. Recent work studies rule learning with LLMs via prompting, extracting rules from demonstrations Gao and Das (2024) , graphs Chen et al. (2024) , or traces Zhang et al. (2024) to guide generation Zhou et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2024b) . Other approaches use rules at training time for synthetic supervision Morishita et al. (2024) , reward modeling Wang and Xiong (2025) , or distillation Sadeq et al. (2025) , or store rules in memory Wang et al. (2024c) . In contrast to these largely static or training-time uses, we learn and consolidate rules from failures for dynamic inference-time reuse. Tool Retrieval and Calling. Tool-use agents often rely on retriever–generator pipelines or finetuning to select and call tools ( Qin et al., 2023 ; Patil et al., 2023 ) , or train models to use tools via self-supervision or agent tuning ( Schick et al., 2023 ; Chen and others, 2024 ; Wu and others, 2024 ) . More recent work tokenizes tools to enable generative retrieval and calling ( Hao et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) . While effective, these approaches encode adaptation in model parameters. We instead externalize adaptation as a compact, symbolic rule library, enabling interpretable, modular reuse across LLMs without retraining.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We propose RimRule , an approach for adapting LLMs by distilling compact, interpretable rules from failure traces and applying them at inference time. Without modifying model weights, our method uses symbolic representations and MDL-guided consolidation to produce reusable rule libraries that improve both in- and out-of-distribution performance, outperform prompting-based methods, and complement finetuned models. These results suggest that inference-time rule learning provides a practical path toward more modular, interpretable, and reusable LLM adaptation.
